items.title: Middle-aged women in England least likely to successfully quit smoking, study finds
items.desc: Of nearly 8,000 women who tried to stop, only 18% of those aged 45 to 60 managed to give up Middle-aged women in England are the least likely to successfully give up smoking, according to research . Smoking is the leading cause of preventable death and illness in the UK. While overall smoking rates in England have declined in recent decades, rates in some regions have increased. About 6.75 million people smoke in England, of whom around 14% are women aged 45-60. Continue reading...

items.title: Latest review of Met police culture finds little has changed since last one
items.desc: Failure to implement previous reports means institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia still present in force Metropolitan police still institutionally racist and misogynist, says report From the Stephen Lawrence inquiry in 1999 to Louise Casey’s landmark review in 2023, successive reports on the Metropolitan police have arrived at the same damning conclusion: Britain’s largest police force is institutionally racist. It will, therefore, come as little surprise that three years after Casey’s report, an independent review led by Gillian Fairfield has found that institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia persist within the force. Continue reading...

items.title: UK to launch world’s first licensing scheme for knife sales
items.desc: Exclusive: Measures aimed at tackling grey market sellers known to sell dangerous knives to children Ministers will introduce the world’s first licensing scheme for businesses and private individuals selling all types of knives including cutlery, the Home Office announced on Wednesday. In a drive to fulfil the government’s pledge to halve knife crime within 10 years, shops and online vendors selling butter knives or machetes will be expected to apply for a licence or face fines. items.title: Metropolitan police still institutionally racist and misogynist, says report

The investigation by Gillian Fairfield found “fundamental, systemic issues” and “institutional defensiveness” still existed in Britain’s biggest police force, which has struggled “to acknowledge racism as a structural problem”. Continue reading...

items.title: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds
items.desc: People from lowest socioeconomic group in all countries studied had higher frailty scores than those in highest socioeconomic group England has the largest gap between higher and lower socioeconomic groups when it comes to frailty compared with 30 other countries, a major study has found. The research, led by academics at King’s College London and published in BMC Medicine, looked at levels of frailty in 71,703 people from 31 countries including England, the US, China, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Greece, Cyprus, Latvia and Lithuania. items.title: Coastal areas in England at risk of erosion to receive £11m in new funding

More than £11m will be shared between 12 council-led projects that will test ways to spot coastal change earlier and help communities plan for the effects. Continue reading...

items.title: Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse
items.desc: PM brings forward changes to non-disclosure agreements and promises consultation on staggered age of consent Men have used wealth and fame to get away with abuse. No longer Andy Burnham has called recent high-profile rape trials a “watershed moment” for the UK and has opened the door to a wider ban on non-disclosure agreements. The prime minister has brought forward changes to NDAs so that from January victims of crimes or workplace harassment will have complete freedom over who they can speak to, even if they have signed an NDA, and he promised the move was “just the start” of a crackdown. Continue reading...

items.title: Burnham launches inquiry into nuclear bomb test veterans’ records
items.desc: Hillsborough panel chair to lead investigation into programme of blood tests during nuclear weapons trials Andy Burnham has launched a Hillsborough-style investigation to examine a programme of blood tests on service personnel during nuclear weapons trials, which he said had been the subject of a “criminal cover-up on an industrial scale”. The Ministry of Defence admitted conducting biological examinations on troops exposed to nuclear testing, having denied it to parliament and the courts for decades. In September, the former defence minister Tobias Ellwood admitted to unwittingly misleading parliament in 2018 over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans . Continue reading...

The Welsh-Indian film-maker’s work, which incorporates themes of memory, migration and hidden histories, was praised by judges for its “restless will to play, experiment and change”. items.title: Outcry grows over Labour plan to exempt most brownfield sites from nature protection rules
items.desc: Chancellor’s decision to exempt plots up to 1.5 hectares allows developers to dodge rules aiming to reverse wildlife declines An outcry is growing over the UK chancellor’s removal of most brownfield housing plots from a legal requirement for developers to measurably enhance nature. John Healey’s decision in the budget to exempt brownfield plots of up to 1.5 hectares from biodiversity net gain (BNG) laws effectively means housing developers of inner-city, urban and surburban sites will be able to dodge rules designed to reverse steep wildlife declines while also allowing housebuilding growth. According to government data, 86% of brownfield sites currently registered are 1.5ha or under. Continue reading...

items.title: Ministers approve fast-track disability payments in England and Wales

The Department for Work and Pensions said on Tuesday it would immediately commit to speeding up the personal independence payment (Pip) system for adults in England and Wales who have severe conditions or ones that are unlikely to change. items.title: ‘It was a cover-up’: HarperCollins accused of using lawyers to shut down concerns about David Walliams
items.desc: Women who spoke to internal investigation about inappropriate behaviour by Walliams still too scared to speak out The publisher HarperCollins used a leading legal firm and a non-disclosure agreement to “cover up” David Walliams’ inappropriate behaviour towards women two years before the children’s author was unexpectedly dropped, according to former staff. Women had complained to the company’s management for years about the author’s alleged misconduct and harassment. The concerns raised included that Walliams had an “inappropriate” sexual relationship with a woman who was an intern when he first met her, had inappropriate interactions with at least three other women connected to the company including asking two for dates, and approached a girl who appeared to be in her teens at a book signing event. Continue reading...
